The following screens have been enabled when migrating Work Patterns from the Back Office into the Portal, but are not currently utilised.

The Standard Hours screen shows you the standard hours in a work pattern and allows you to add and sequence the hours as well as adding extra information using the 3-dot menu.
Breaks
The Breaks Screen lets you view and add break patterns in a sequence. You can also configure clockings or penalties for employees and teams.
Absence
The Absence Screen is a new screen which amalgamates all the previous absence screens and bringing them all together in one place. It allows you to configure full and part day values as well as configure manager approval.
Overtime
The Overtime screen centralises all of the previous overtime options from the Back Office together on one screen.
Flexitime Settings
The Flexitime screen amalgamates all the previous flexitime settings from the Back Office on to one screen and includes adding new sequence items.
Alternate Patterns
The Alternate Patterns screen has amalgamated Alternate pattern information and creation in to one screen
Premiums
The Premiums Screen is in two parts. The main information displayed on the fixed left-hand side of the screen such as the Worked Pay code and Thresholds. Additional settings are shown on the scrolling right-hand side of the screen allow you to view more detailed information.

All rostering configuration is now amalgamated on the Rostering Screen, having been migrated from the Back Office.

Background

A Holiday Scheme is a list of closure dates, such as public/bank holidays and departmental fixed closure days. These dates will be treated as non-working days for anyone linked to the Holiday Scheme (via their Balance). The system using employee work schedules to determine if the employee would normally work on the closure day and adjusts their entitlement accordingly. 

A Holiday scheme can be linked to a Balance, but this is optional and Balances will function without a Holiday Scheme. Holiday Schemes should not be used with Accrual Balances. 

A single Holiday Scheme can be linked to multiple Balances with:

Different FTE Hours 
Different Long Service Schemes
Different leave years
Different Base Entitlement
All Balances linked to a Holiday Scheme must share the same:

Mandatory holiday dates (e.g. public holiday and fixed closure dates)

To complete this function menu profile WFM_BANK_HOLIDAY_CONFIG must be assigned to the individual portal user via Security > User Management.

Overview
This document has been written to detail the customer specific configuration required to implement the Workforce Management module of People XD from the Access Software Suite at 5 pilot sites at the University of Oxford. 
The broad in-scope processes are as follows:
Occupational Absence
Leave Management
Leave Management (Accruals)
Online Timesheet Claims
Pilot Departments
Throughout the Discovery process, the following departments have been confirmed as pilot groups:
Classics
BDI-NDM
Oxford Ludwig Institute NDM
Physics – Lab Demonstrators
Human Resources

The breakdown of employees in each pilot site is as follows:

Full Time/Part Time, Part Time Term Time employees having the Occupational Absence and Leave Management functionality.
Variable Hours and Casual employees having Leave Management (Accrual) and Online Timesheet Claims functionality.
Introduction
Oxford University are introducing Occupational Absence, Leave Management and Online Timesheet Claims to four Departments within Oxford.
Full Time/Part Time, Part Time Term Time employees having the Occupational Absence and Leave Management functionality.
Variable Hours and Casual employees having Leave Management (Accrual) and Online Timesheet Claims functionality.
During the Discovery Process, Reference Data was gathered from the University to be used within the configuration of the system. 
The remainder of this document describes how that data has been utilised in the configuration and where areas of the system link to other areas of the system.

1. Reference Data Configuration
1.1 Company Details
The Company details determine the name of the Time Company and the ‘Day’ of the week in which Schedules begin.
Oxford have confirmed that the start day of the week is a Monday. 
The Company has been configured as follows:

1.2 Calendar 
1.2.1 System Calendar
The System Calendar underpins the system and is probably the most important area of the system to maintain.
The System Calendar is used within the following areas of the system:
System Calendar, which would be used by any weekly paid employees, 
Team Scheduler in Portal, ensuring the Team Scheduler opens on the real time week on a Monday
Timesheet in Portal, ensuring employees see Monday as the beginning of the week
Shift Type Reference Data, ensuring all Shift Types configured begin on a Monday

The System Calendar has been extended until the end of 2022. Beyond this, the calendar will require extension into the future. It is recommended that this calendar is extended yearly as part of the balance year end process. 

1.2.2 User Defined Calendar
In addition to the System Calendar, Oxford have requested the use of a User Defined Calendar (UDC). The UDC is used in the following areas of the system:
Work Group to ensure that all employees contained in a Work Group that is configured as a UDC Work Group have their Online Timesheet Claims paid in accordance to the open calendar period
Approval Process, ensuring any timesheets requiring Approval are visible
Sign Off Process, ensuring any timesheets requiring Approval are visible
Generate Timesheet, ensuring only timesheets for the open calendar period are transferred from CoreTime to CorePay for payment.

1.8 Work Patterns 
A Work Pattern is how the employees’ day is shaped based on a number of hours/minutes worked in a day. Work Patterns are used in the Shift Types to create Shift Types relevant to the employees working week.
Work Patterns are used to determine the number of hours an employee would:
Be scheduled to work
Be deducted from an Annual Leave Balance
Be recorded for Occupational Absence
Included in the Calendar on the Employee Portal Dashboard
All employee who are not Casual should be awarded a Shift Type containing Work Patterns that are identical to their normal working week. Casuals will be assigned a Shift Type of CASUAL as they will not be recording Absences (see Occupational Absence section) and Annual Leave (see Balances section) is based on an Accrual Balance.
Configured within the system is a Work Pattern for every 5 minute increment between 0 hrs and 12 hrs.

As staff at the University don’t clock in and out, all Start Times have been set to 9am. Each of the Work Patterns also contains a Default Pay Code of 3600 – Normal Attendance, meaning that this will not be passed to Payroll.
Casuals have a Work Pattern of REST, which has been utilised in the Shift Type of CASUAL. This will allow CASUALs to book time withing the Online Timesheet Claims functionality and it pass through to Payroll.

1.11 Balances
The Discovery process identified five different Balances to accommodate the different Departments in the Pilot. Each Balance has slightly different requirements to accommodate the Employee Annual Leave Entitlements.
The Balances are:

Navigation to the Balance Configuration is found:
CoreTime/Roster > System Param > Balance (all sub menus are from this path)
1.11.1 Balances with Entitlements
For Balances ACDEP1, ACDEP2, NDM1, NDM2, UAS1 and UAS2, the Balances have been configured as an ‘with Entitlements’ type Balance.
1.11.1.1 Balance Parameters
The Balance configuration includes functionality that will not allow employees to enter into negative Annual Leave Balances, Rounding to the nearest .50 (Deci) of an hour.
The calculation of the Annual Leave Balance for a new employee is computed automatically as follows:
Annual Leave Entitlement/365.25 x Number of Calendar Days left in the Annual Leave Balance Year, rounded up to the nearest ½ hour.
Each Balance has been configured to display o the Manager Portal in the following area:
Portal > Manager Dashboard> WFM Page > Balances
1.11.1.2 Balances Calendars
Each of the Balances above have been assigned a Calendar in line with the University’s academic year. The academic year runs from October to September each year.
The system has been configured to 2022, and future years will need to be administered by the University.
1.11.1.3 Balances Entitlements
Each of the above Balances has an entitlement in both Days and Hours, with a Long Service Award assigned to each (see Section 1.11.3 below)
When deploying the Balance to each employee, the University have made the decision to deploy in hours.
1.11.1.4 Balance Pro-Ration
Balance Pro-Ration has been administered in the process to ensure that only employees with an Employee Status of Permanent, Fixed Term, Pensioner, Leaver, Open Ended Externally Funded, Self- Financing and Worker. All other Employment Status Types are excluded from the pro-ration and are not entitled to the Balance.
1.11.2 Balances with Accruals
For Balances CASUAL and VARI, these Balances have been configured differently. These Balances will be assigned to Variable Contract employees and Casual Employees.
1.11.2.1 Balance Parameters
The Balance configuration includes functionality that will not allow employees to enter into negative Annual Leave Balances, Rounding to the nearest .50 (Deci) of an hour. 
The calculation of the Annual Leave Balance for a new employee is computed automatically as follows:
Approved Hours in Timesheet x % applied to the Annual Leave Scheme = Total Hours Accrued
Each Balance has been configured to display o the Manager Portal in the following area:
Portal > Manager Dashboard> WFM Page > Balances
1.11.2.2 Balances Calendars
The Balance Calendar is a rolling Calendar and contains the percentage of the Accrual.
In addition, each employee will have a Personal Calendar administered by the University. The dates of the Personal Calendar should be entered at the point of Onboarding or the beginning of a new Appointment.
1.11.2.3 Balances Entitlements
The Balance begins with a zero entitlement and has accrual configuration whereby for each hour recorded in an Online Timesheet Claim, a percentage of those hours is added into the Balance Entitlement.
1.11.2.4 Balances Accrual Pay Codes
For each of the Pay Codes identified by the University for employees to book worked hours against within a timesheet, have also been added into the Accrual Pay Codes within the Balance. This will ensure that for each of the hours booked against a Pay Code contained in the list, a percentage of the hours will be added to the Balance.
1.11.3 Long Service Awards
Long Service Awards have been added to each of the Balances that have an entitlement, along with the Variable Hours Scheme.
1.11.3.1 Long Service Awards for Balances with Entitlements
Each Long Service Award Scheme has been added in hours. The scheme rules are contained within the configuration and also within the IG.

1.11.4 Pro rata entitlements

Each balance will require each employee status set up to apply a pro rata starting entitlement. The path to this is:

1.12 Holiday Schemes 
During Discovery it was highlighted that the different Departments within the University have different Public Holidays and Company Closure Days.
To ensure that employees are treated to these days off, the dates of the Public Holidays and Company Closure Days have been configured into the Holiday Schemes.
The hours relative to these have been deducted from the employee’s entitlement, leaving just the days left to take at their leisure.
There are three different Holiday Schemes for the different Departments and will only apply to those Departments where employees have been granted a Balance with Entitlements.
By adding the Holiday Scheme to the Annual Leave Balance, the system computes the Annual Leave Balance as follows:
Balance Entitlement from Annual Leave Scheme + Public Holidays/Company Closure Days – any days taken = Remaining Entitlement.
The Holiday Scheme dates have been configured in accordance with those provided in the IG. However, this area of the system will require ongoing maintenance for future years for both the Company Closure Days and the Public Holidays.
1.13 Balance Year End 
At the end of each Balance Year, the Balance Calendars for all Annual Leave Schemes should be updated to accommodate the future year and in addition, the Holiday Scheme Calendar should be updated with the Public Holidays and Company Closure Dates per Scheme.
Balance Year End should be run on 1st October (immediately after the last day of the previous Balance Year for all schemes that are not a rolling Balance).
Navigation: CoreTime/Roster > Period End > Generate Balance Period End
Please see Documentation on the University for Generating Balance Period End.

2. Person Configuration
There will be, on occasion, the need to override default configuration that has been applied within the Reference Data, so that employees do not inherit the default, but an alternative setting accurate to their employment period.
The application of these overrides can be completed within two areas of the system:
Back Office – Person Maintenance
Portal – People Management Dashboard
2.1 Person Overrides 
With Back Office, from the Person Maintenance menu option, certain default configuration can be overridden for an employee.
2.2.1 Holiday Scheme Override – Back Office
The Holiday Scheme is configured within the Work Group and will apply to all employees contained within it.
To override the Holiday Scheme to that of a different one, the path is:
CoreTime/Roster > Person Data > Pers Maintenance > locate Employee > Work Group Override
And choose the Holiday Scheme relevant to the employee
2.2 Person Additional Configuration for Time - Portal
When Onboarding an employee, or adding a new Contract, or Changing a Current Contract, there are three additional areas within the People Management Dashboard that will need to be added/updated.
2.2.1 Personalised Pay Code Groups
For each employee included in the Pilot Departments, a Personalised Pay Code Group (PPCG) will need to be assigned to their Personnel Record.
The PPCG should be relevant to the Post that they are performing and not to the Person.
NB: an employee with 4 or 5 different Posts may have 4 or 5 different PPCGs depending on the post they are performing.
2.2.2 Shift Type
For each employee included in the Pilot Departments, a Shift Type will need to be assigned to the employee. If the employees Shift Type is not that of the default set on the Work Group, the Shift Type should be added as part of the Onboarding / Contract Change to reflect their working week.
2.2.3 Balance Entitlement
When Onboarding a new employee, depending on the Department that they are assigned to and their Contractual Hours per week, an Annual Leave Balance should be assigned to their Personnel Record. If the Employee is of a CASUAL / VARIABLE Hours type contract, they should be assigned the appropriate Balance and the Personal Calendar completed within their Personnel Record
2.2.4 Absence Category
Absence Categories are no longer required due to the de-scoping of the Occupational Absence transferring to CorePay
2.3 Organisational Roles by Person
The Organisational Roles by Person determines the roles that are assigned to Managers of Work Groups.
Each non-Pilot Manager should have the Reports to Role as 001 – Manager. This will allow access to the employees of their Work Group
Each Pilot Manager should have a ‘Reports to’ for their Work Group, the Role name being ‘Pilot Manager Absence and Delegation. This will provide the Manager with access to their Employees within Portal.
In addition to this role, if the Manager is looking after employees Annual Leave requests, they will also require ‘Leave Approver’ Role. This will be the standard two roles that should be applied to Managers, unless they wish to re-direct on a permanent basis their Leave Approvals to a dedicated Leave Approver.

In addition to the above, where the Manager of the Work Group is assigned to a Work Group containing some or all employees that will use the new Online Timesheet Claims process, they will have an additional role of TS_APP. This role provides access to allow the Manager to receive Online Timesheet Claims from employees. 
2.4 Menu Profiles
2.4.1 Manager Menu Profiles
NON-PILOT MANAGERS
For non-Pilot Managers, the Menu Profile that should be assigned to them is COREPORTAL_MANAGER. The COREPORTAL_MANAGER Menu Profile does not allow access to the Scheduler nor the Absence Module. D

PILOT MANAGERS
There are three new Menu Profiles that have been created for the Managers as part of this Pilot. The two profiles are:
COREPORTAL_LEAVE_APPROVER
COREPORTAL_TS_CLAIM_MGR
As with the Organisational Roles by Person, the COREPORTAL_LEAVE_APPROVER should be assigned to the Manager if they are managing their Employees Leave Approvals, and if they are also managing the Online Timesheet Claims, they should be assigned the COREPORTAL_TS_CLAIM_MGR.
There is one new Menu Profile that has been created for the Managers as part of this Pilot. The new profile is:
COREPORTAL_MANAGER_TIME
The above profile when assigned to an employee will provide access to the following functionality:
My Approvals (functionality and Widget)
Manager Timesheet Summary (functionality and Widget)
Delegation
The COREPORTAL_MANAGER_TIME Menu Profile can also be granted to a non-manager for Delegation purposes by assigning the DEL Organisational Role to a designated employee along with the Work Group they will be a Delegate for. The Menu Profile is assigned during an overnight job triggered by having the relevant Employment Status listed in the Menu Profile Matrix and the employee being assigned the Role of DEL.
2.4.2 Employee Menu Profiles
As part of the Pilot project, additional Menu Profiles have been created for the employees to grant access to the Online Timesheet Claim process, Book Leave and Balance Management. The Menu Profiles COREPORTAL_TS_CLAIM_EMP, COREPORTAL_EMPLOYEE_BALANCE and COREPORTAL_EMPLOYEE_BOOK_LEAVE should only be granted to employees who will be authorised to claim worked hours via the Online Timesheet Claims process, Book Leave or Manage their Balance.

2.5 CoreTime System Users
The CoreTime System User from the original implementation has been continued throughout the T&A implementation process in terms of Manager Access. Additional Configuration of the CoreTime System Users has enabled the TS_APP for the Timesheets and LEAVE for the Leave Approval.
Each of the above have the relevant configuration to allow access to the Managers that have these Organisational Roles applied to their record.
There is only one Organisational Role for 001, LEAVE and TS_APP meaning that if a Manger is to complete this role, they should be granted the role via Maintain Organisational Roles by Person.
There is not a requirement to create a Back Office System User Account per Manager, they will all use the same settings from the Organisational Role.
Employees requiring access to Insight Reporting will need to have a MSS account created using their Employee Number as the Username and the relevant Work Groups the Employee requires access to.

3. Generate Timesheets
The Generate Timesheet process is the ‘interface’ between CoreTime and CorePay where Timesheets within the system for a selected time period are generated and passed to Pay.
The Process for this is based on several areas of the system:
Work Group having the correct calendar attached
Work Group enabled for Generate Timesheets
UDC in the Calendar has the correct open month
All Timesheets for the period are Approved
All Timesheets for the period are Signed Off
3.1 Approval Process
The Approval Process has been configured to be administered by the Timesheet Approver in Portal as part of the Online Timesheet Claim Process. The Portal Approval Process will cover both tasks – Approve and Sign Off.
Employees who have Admin access can also Approve Hours if required via Back Office.
Navigation: CoreTime/Roster > Time Management > Approve Hours > add in Calendar 

3.2 Sign Off Process
Within the BackOffice functionality, there is provision for Administrators to be able to Sign Off any Unconfirmed Hours that should prevent the Generate Timesheet Process. 
For the University, configuration has been requested to allow Unconfirmed Timesheets to ROLL OVER until Approve/Sign Off process has been completed within the Online Timesheet Claim process by the Timesheet Approver. 
Navigation: CoreTime/Roster > Time Management > Sign Off Hours

3.2.1 Admin Sign Off in Portal
Sign off for Admins is now available in Portal. For access to this the admin will require:
1. A CoreTime system user with generate timesheets set to All Companies
2. The menu profile WFM_ADMIN_SIGNOFF
The sign off screen is found under WFM Admin Dashboard
Admins can now view any time submissions that have not yet been approved. Admins should either approve and enter a comment saying that an admin has approved the hours or remove the hours submitted and enter their own line of hours. This way would then remove the workflow aspect. Admins can approve and then sign off the hours which will then go through for payment. 
If an admin approves the original entry, then bear in mind that the workflow will not drop off the employee or the manager’s dashboard. A manager can approve this workflow at a later date but it will have no impact as the hours had already been paid. 
N.B: Admin access in sign off screen is only limited by the system user having generate timesheets on all companies. Admins will see all hours, not just those to the specific work group and department access granted by the system user set up.
3.3 Ignore Unconfirmed Hours (Un-Signed off Hours)
Functionality has been enabled to allow Timesheets that have been submitted within a specific time frame that remain unconfirmed at the point of generating timesheets into pay to be allowed to roll over to the next month.
When rolling the hours into the next month, the system will automatically update the Payroll Period so that the hours are displayed with the new period within the system.
The system uses the ‘Countback’ weeks to determine how many months these hours can be rolled forward for and once exhausted will not include the hours in any roll forward periods.

3.4 Generate Timesheet – inc. Ignore Unconfirmed Hours
The Generate Timesheet Process is the process from transferring Online Timesheet Claims from CoreTime to CorePay using a specific set of dates laid out within the User Defined Calendar.
There are two modes of generation – Test and Live explained below
3.4.1 Generate Timesheet – Test Mode
When generating the Timesheet in TEST Mode, the system will automatically draw in all Online Timesheet Claims for the open month within the User Defined Calendar.
In Test Mode, the Generate Timesheet process can be run as many times as required, and for all combinations of Work Groups:
Single Work Group
Selection of Work Groups
All Work Groups.
Once generated and the payroll processes have been run to the stage of Gross To Net, the Timesheets can be seen in the Timesheet area of the Employee Record, or in the Gross to Net Screen.
Navigation: CoreTime Roster > Period End > Generate Timesheets

3.4.2 Generate Timesheet – LIVE Mode
The Timesheets should never be generated in LIVE mode until the very last run and all checks have taken place ready for payment.
When the Timesheets are run in Live Mode, the system will:
Generate the Timesheets for Payment and transfer into CorePay
Update the User Defined Calendar to the next process period
Update the CoreTime Input Period for any Unconfirmed Hours
Once the Generate Timesheet process has been run in Live, there is not an option to reverse back to the previous month.

4. Occupational Absence
The Occupational Absence Module that sits between CoreTime and CorePay and transfers the Absences entered by Managers either via Portal or Back Office directly into CorePay has been de-activated.
This will mean that Managers and Admins may record Absences in CoreTime, but they will only be used for recording purposes and will require a report to gain the information.
No calculations relating to entitlement will be performed by the system.

The Workgroup Override allows the user to override certain workgroup settings at an employee level.

Context
A data source is technically the source of the data which is returned by a report query, i.e. the PeopleXD database which powers your reports (UOXC, UOXP, etc.). In Visual Studio, though, the term “data source” refers to something more like a connection profile – it’s where you both define which PeopleXD database you’re going to use, and provide the login credentials for accessing that database. 
There are two shared data sources held in all of the HR Reporting Visual Studio solutions and used across the majority of reports: 

Oracle_DS_ServiceAccount: This data source is linked to a PeopleXD service account rather than a standard user account. It is primarily used to run the SQL queries for the shared datasets which populate report parameters, e.g. to retrieve all department codes for use in a parameter’s drop-down list.

Oracle_DS_UserCredentials: This data source relies on each user’s individual reporting login credentials. When a user enters their credentials and runs a report, the PeopleXD database will automatically apply the correct user security to the data when retrieving the report results; e.g. a user who is only allowed to see Pay Group 20 will only see results for Pay Group 20.
Viewing data sources
To view a shared data source, go to the Solution Explorer pane in your Visual Studio solution and expand the Shared Data Sources folder. You will be presented with a list of data sources currently available within the solution.

Double-click or right-click the data source you wish to view and select Open from the menu: 

The Shared Data Source Properties window will open and the General screen will be displayed. 

Database connection
The “Connection String” field will show you which PeopleXD database the current Visual Studio solution is connected to, e.g. UOXZ, UOXC, UOXU or UOXP. This is the database from which all reports in the current solution will retrieve their data: 

Login credentials
Each data source connects to PeopleXD by logging into the database specified in the “Connection String”. This means that login credentials must be supplied to the data source. 
To check the login credentials for a data source, click Build… next to the “Connection String” field: 

The Connection Properties window will pop up. This window will confirm which PeopleXD database the data source is using in the “Server name” field, along with the login credentials being used to access that database. You can check whether the data source is able to access the database with the login credentials provided by clicking “Test Connection”:

Visual Studio will supply the login credentials to PeopleXD and confirm whether the database is accessible: 

If you have entered invalid login credentials, the connection test will fail when Visual Studio attempts to access the PeopleXD database:

Double-check the username and password you’ve entered and try testing the connection again. If you are still unable to connect to the PeopleXD database, a couple of things might be happening:

The PeopleXD reporting database is unavailable – the databases occasionally become uncontactable, for instance during system maintenance. If this is the case, nobody should be able to log into the reporting database in question. Speak to another HR Reporting Visual Studio user and ask them to test their connection to the same data source. If they are able to connect to the data source and you still can’t, you probably need to reset your password. 
Your HR Reporting password has expired – if this is the case, you will need to contact the HR Systems Support team and get your HR reporting password reset. Be sure to specify which PeopleXD database you are trying to access, so that your password can be reset in the correct environment. 

Amending data sources

Amending in Visual Studio

NB: If you have reset your HR Reporting password, you will need to update it in the Oracle_DS_UserCredentials data source. 
If you need to amend a data source in Visual Studio, go to the Solution Explorer pane in your Visual Studio solution and expand the Shared Data Sources folder. 

Select and open the shared data source you wish to amend. The Shared Data Source Properties window will open and the General screen will be displayed. 

Click Build… next to the “Connection String” field to open the Connection Properties window: 

You can now edit the data source’s database connection or login credentials as required. 
Database connection
To amend the database connection for a data source, update the value in the “Server name” field to indicate which PeopleXD database you wish to connect to.
Example: If your data source previously connected to the UOXU database and you want it to connect to UOXP, enter “UOXP” in the “Server name” field:

Supply the relevant login credentials and click “Test Connection” to check that you are able to access the new database. 

Login credentials
To update the login credentials for a data source, amend the values in the “User name” and/or “Password” fields: 

Click “Test Connection” to check that you are able to access the database with the new login credentials.

NOTES: The UserCredentials data source 
For the Oracle_DS_UserCredentials data source, the login credentials can be set to your personal reporting login details – this will enable you to run your report in the Preview pane without having to provide your username and password every time you want to run queries in Visual Studio. 
Just enter your login details in the Connection Properties window and select “Save my password” to store your password for the duration of your Visual Studio session. 

NOTES: The ServiceAccount data source
For the Oracle_DS_ServiceAccount data source, the login credentials are the same across all Visual Studio solutions and the “Save my password” option is selected in each instance so that the login credentials don’t need to be refreshed: 

If for whatever reason you need to re-enter the login credentials for the ServiceAccount data source, the username is “REPORT_POWERBI”. See the note about the password below. 

NB: The Service Account has unlimited user sessions and unrestricted access to PeopleXD’s databases, so it must be kept highly secure to prevent unwanted data breaches. Only a subset of reporting super-users (Athena Artuso and Simon Burford) know the login credentials for the ServiceAccount data source, and they must periodically update these login credentials to keep the account secure. 
If you need to add the password for the Oracle_DS_ServiceAccount data source to your Visual Studio solution, you must contact Athena or Simon and ask them to update the data source for you. 

Amending on the SQL Server
Once the data sources have been amended in Visual Studio and you have checked that the change has worked you can make the change on the SQL Server. To do this you must not attempt to redeploy the data source from Visual Studio, instead make the changes manually.
To do this, navigate to the Data Sources folder on the SQL Server (you may need to display hidden folders if you haven’t already):
For each data source, click on the ellipsis and select “Manage”:
Amend the database name within the connection string:
You may also need to enter the credentials if you are amending the Oracle_DS_ServiceAccount data source, if so, test that you have entered them correctly.
Finally click on the “Apply” button at the bottom of the screen.
Updating the HRIS Launcher
If you have re-pointed an SQL server to a different PeopleXD environment you should update the text on the HRIS Launcher page which explains which PeopleXD environment each HR Reporting environment is pointed at:

To alter this, open Notepad++ and open:
O:/PS/HR Systems/Support/Infrastructure/HRIS Launcher/HRIS_launcher.html
Search for the HR Reporting Environment to amend, you can search for the following phrase to search for the QA environment, for example:
<!-- Pointing Dates for QA -->
When you have updated the environment and the date you made the change, update the date the page was updated and save your changes. You can find the last updated date by searching for the following phrase:
<!-- last updated on -->
Adding data sources to reports
Most .RDL files in Visual Studio must contain the two standard shared data sources: the ServiceAccount source and the UserCredentials source. 

To check which data sources are attached to your .RDL file, go to the Report Data pane on the left side of the screen and open the Data Sources folder:

If you are missing either data source, simply right-click the Data Sources folder and select Add Data Source…. 

The Data Source Properties window will open. Select the radio button to “Use shared data source reference” and select the appropriate data source from the drop-down menu:

Edit the “Name” field to match the name of the shared data source:

Click “OK” to confirm your change. Remember to click the “Save” icon before closing your .RDL file or your changes won’t be saved!

Removing data sources from reports
It is highly unlikely that you will ever need to remove a data source from a report, however if you do need to, go to the Report Data pane on the left side of the screen and open the Data Sources folder:

Right-click the data source you wish to remove and click “Delete”:

Save your changes before closing the .RDL file.

Report files (.RDLs)

The Reports folder
Go to the Solution Explorer pane and expand the Reports folder. You will be presented with a list of the report files currently available to open within the solution. 

NB: This is not the total list of existing .RDL files within a solution. Visual Studio will only display a limited number of files in the Solution Explorer pane, but you can add existing .RDL files to the Solution Explorer pane by following the steps below. 

If you want to view an existing .RDL file but do not see it displayed in the Solution Explorer, you can add it into the Solution Explorer by going to the Reports folder and right-clicking it. Select Add > Existing Item… (or type Shift + Alt + A):

The solution folder on I:\OUIT\CoreHR Reports will open. This folder contains all the files which belong to the solution that you are currently working in: 

If you want to add an .RDL file from a different solution, navigate back to the main I:\OUIT\CoreHR Reports folder and select the solution file you want to open. You can see from the title bar and the file path here that you are selecting files from the DEV solution to add them to the QA solution:

Scroll through the solution folder until you find the file you want to add to the Solution Explorer, then select it and click Add:

The file you have added will now appear at the bottom of the Reports list within the Solution Explorer:

Opening a report (.RDL)
To open an .RDL, scroll to it in the Solution Explorer pane and either double-click it, or right-click and select Open from the menu:

The .RDL file will load and the report’s Design pane will be displayed.

The Design pane
All .RDL files within Visual Studio have a Design pane, where you can format the data from your SQL query into a user-friendly report. The Design pane for every report in the HR Reporting catalogue must contain the following elements:
Parameter fields
If your report has parameters, these must appear above the report as interactive fields (free-text, drop-down, or date/time). 

NB: If your report does not have interactive parameter fields, users will not be prompted to enter parameters when they run the report.
Title textbox 
This textbox appears at the top of the report and contains the title of the .RDL file, in the format [Report prefix] + [.RDL name], e.g. PERDEP01 Limited Data Set. 

Parameters textbox 
This textbox appears underneath the Title, and contains a VBA expression which will display the parameters a user has selected each time the report is run. In the Design pane, it looks like this:

When a report has been run, the Parameters textbox looks like this:

Report Tablix
The “Tablix” (a Microsoft term) displays report data from a data set in cells that are organized into rows and columns. This is where your report fields are arranged and formatted, and where your results appear when you run the report query. A Tablix can be formatted as a simple table or as a matrix. 

Footer textbox
This textbox appears at the bottom of the screen, and contains a standard VBA expression which will display a message whenever the report is run. The message states the name of the .RDL file, the SSO of the username who ran the report, as well as the date and time of the report run. In the Design pane, it looks like this:

When a report has been run, the Footer textbox looks like this:

The Preview pane
All .RDL files within Visual Studio also have a Preview pane, where you can run your report query and check your results and your formatting without needing to deploy the report to the HR Reporting environments. 

To open the Preview pane, simply click the tab at the top of the .RDL file. If your report has parameters, you will be prompted to fill them in, exactly as a report user would be on the HR Reporting environments:

Enter the parameters you wish to use (or none if you don’t want to restrict your results), and click View Report to run the report query. The SQL code of your report will query the PeopleXD database to which your solution is connected, and the “Loading…” message will display while the query runs:

When the query is complete, the report results will load in the Preview pane. The page numbers at the top of the report indicate how many pages of results have been retrieved. 

NB: The parameter prompts at the top of the screen can be edited if you want to re-run the report with new parameters – simply change the parameter values and click View Report to re-run your query.

You can export your results by clicking the Save icon and choosing the export file format: 

To exit the Preview pane, simply click back into the Design tab at the top of the .RDL file. 

NB: Do not click back into the Design pane while the Preview pane is in “Loading…” mode – doing so often causes Visual Studio to freeze up and become non-responsive. 

The Report Data pane
The Report Data pane is where you configure the individual elements of your .RDL file: its data sources, datasets, and parameters. The Report Data pane is located on the left side of the screen:

Expand any of the folders to view their contents. A brief description of each is given below.

NB: The Built-in Fields are essential components of all .RDL files, and are included as standard in every report. We don’t ever edit these values. We also don’t use the Images functionality within Visual Studio, so this folder can be ignored. 

Parameters 
The Parameters folder lists each parameter present in your report. 

You can click into each parameter to view or edit its properties. Double-clicking a parameter will open the Report Parameter Properties window for that specific parameter, where you can view the parameter name, prompt text, data type, available values, and default values (if these have been set). 

Data Sources
The Data Sources folder lists each data source present in your report. All reports must contain the two standard shared data sources:
Oracle_DS_ServiceAccount: the service account is used to run the queries for shared datasets, e.g. to retrieve all department codes for use in a parameter’s drop-down list. 
Oracle_DS_UserCredentials: the user account is used to run the main report SQL code – it’s each report user’s individual reporting login credentials. By passing these credentials to PeopleXD, the database can automatically detect and apply the correct security when retrieving report results; e.g. a user who is only allowed to see Pay Group 20 will only see results for Pay Group 20. 

If you are missing either data source (for instance, if you are creating a new report), simply right-click the Data Sources folder and select Add Data Source…. 

Datasets
The Datasets folder lists each dataset present in your .RDL file. This includes the main report query, as well as any additional datasets which are used to power your parameters. 

NB: The main report query should always be named “DataSet1”, while any parameter-related datasets should have descriptive names linking them to their parameters, e.g. Department for a dataset which provides a list of departments for the Department parameter. 

Double-click any dataset to open the Dataset Properties window. 

If you are looking at an embedded dataset, you can view the raw SQL code of the dataset in the Query pane:

If you are looking at a shared dataset, you will be able to see the full name of the shared dataset – this will enable you to select the shared dataset from the Solution Explorer pane to view the SQL code for that dataset.

Context
A parameter is technically “a limit or boundary which defines the scope of a particular process or activity”. Within the context of HR Reporting, parameters are values a report user can set before running a report. These values limit the query the report sends to the database, and therefore limit the data the report will return from the database.
Example: A report has a parameter for Department Code, which gives the user the option to select specific department codes for which they want to see results when they run the report. Let’s say they select code “AC”: 

When the user clicks “View Report”, the report query will run. Because the user has selected code “AC”, the report query will only check the PeopleXD database for personnel records related to that department code. When the report is finished running, it will only display results for department code “AC”. 

Example: A report has a parameter for Personnel Number, which gives the user the option to specify a personnel record for which they want to see results when they run the report. Let’s say they enter personnel number “2367246”:

When the user clicks “View Report”, the report query will run. Because the user has specified personnel number “2367246”, the report query will only check the PeopleXD database for information related to that personnel number. When the report is finished running, it will only display results for personnel number “2367246”. 
Report parameters are managed in three separate places:
The SQL code of the report query in the .RDL file: essential
The Parameters folder of the Report Data pane: essential 
The Parameters textbox: optional (if the parameter values should be displayed at the top of the report each time it is run)

See below for detailed guidance. 
Viewing a parameter
Parameters exist within report (.RDL) files, so to view the parameters for a report, you will need to open the .RDL file whose parameters you wish to view. 
Within the SQL code
To see the parameters within a report’s SQL code, go to the Report Data pane. Expand the Datasets folder and select “DataSet1” – this is where the report query SQL code is held. 

Double-click to open “DataSet1”. The Dataset Properties window will pop up. Go to the Query pane in the lower half of the window to see the SQL code for the report:

If the report has parameters, they will be listed in “WHERE” clauses within the SQL code, and they will always be in the format :ParameterName.

In Oracle SQL, the colon (:) is what prompts the report query to check for a user-defined value before executing the query. All parameter names must be preceded by a colon.
You can scroll down the Query pane to find the parameters within the SQL code, or you can copy the contents of the Query pane into a Notepad file and do a search for “:” to jump quickly to any parameters in the code: 

Within the Parameters folder
All the parameters present in the .RDL SQL query will also be present in the Parameters folder of the Report Data pane. Simply expand the folder to see the list of parameters:

You can click into each parameter to view its properties. You can also access parameters within the section at the top of the Design pane – simply double-click the parameter you wish to view: 

Double-clicking a parameter in either the Report Data pane or the Design pane will open the Report Parameter Properties window for that specific parameter.

There are three main aspects to any parameter: General, Available Values, and Default Values. You can view these by clicking the tabs at the side of the Report Parameter Properties window. 
General: this tab defines the name of the parameter, the prompt a user sees when running the report, what type of data the parameter will accept, and whether or not the parameter should be visible to users.
Available Values: this tab defines the list of values (LOV) which can be passed to a parameter, e.g. a list of department codes. If Available Values are defined, the parameter will only accept values from that list. 
Default Values: this tab defines what value(s) should automatically be passed to the parameter whenever a report is opened. Users can change the default value to something specific; the default is just present to save people time, so they don’t always have to select the most commonly-used values for a parameter. 
Within the Parameters textbox 
Most reports include a textbox above the Tablix in the Design pane which will display the selected parameters after the report is run.

Here’s an example of how that looks on a report which has just been run: 

Within the .RDL file’s Design pane, the textbox looks like this:

To view how the parameters are set up in the textbox, right-click it and select “Expression”: 

The Expression window will pop up. Within this window, you can see the VBA code which determines how each parameter is displayed within the textbox when the report is run. 

NB: Not all parameters are displayed in the textbox! “Username”, for instance, is never included here. 

If a parameter is included in the textbox, it will appear as part of a “+” statement; e.g. this statement, which shows the DepartmentCode parameter for a report: 

+ iif(Parameters!DepartmentCode.Value="","Department code : '< All department codes >'","Department code : '" + Parameters!DepartmentCode.Value + "' ")

What the code is saying
The VBA code here is just an IF-THEN-ELSE statement and can be understood as follows: 

IF the DepartmentCode parameter is blank (Value = “”), THEN the textbox should display the string “Department code: ‘< All department codes >’”.
ELSE if the DepartmentCode parameter is not blank, the textbox should look at whatever values have been selected for the DepartmentCode parameter, and display the string “Department code: ‘[parameter value1, parameter value2,…]’”. 

The majority of parameters in the textbox will be written in this format. See below for more guidance. 

Creating a new parameter
Within the SQL code
To add a new parameter to the SQL code of the .RDL file, you will need to modify the appropriate “WHERE” clause within the code. Some reports contain only one “WHERE” clause, but complex reports may contain several, as conditions and parameters are applied to the query at different stages. 
Decide where in the SQL you want to add the parameter, then add it to the “WHERE” clause in one of the following formats:
For parameters which use a drop-down LOV…

Format: (VIEW.ITEM IN (:Parameter) OR ‘-1’ IN (:Parameter))
Example: (prbi_appointment_history.department_description IN (:Department) OR '-1' IN (:Department))
For parameters which use a free-text field (single value)…

Format: (VIEW.ITEM = (:Parameter) OR (:Parameter) IS NULL)
Example: (prbi_hr_person_master.person_reference=(:PersonRef) OR (:PersonRef) IS NULL)
For parameters which use a free-text field (multi-value), see the Appendix.
Once you’ve modified the SQL, be sure to save your changes to the .RDL file.

Within the Parameters folder
Go to the Parameters folder of the Report Data pane. Right-click and select “Add Parameter…”

You can also create parameters within the section at the top of the Design pane. This is a little table which contains the parameters in rows and columns. 

To add a parameter to this table, right-click an empty cell (like the one highlighted below) and select “Add Parameter…”.

What if there aren’t any empty cells?
If you want to add a parameter to a report but there are no empty cells in the parameters table at the top of the Design pane, you can add a new row or column to the table. Simply right-click an existing row or column and select whether (and where) you would like to add your new row or column:

Once you’ve added the new row/column, you can right-click any of the empty cells and select “Add Parameter…” to create your new parameter.
After you click “Add Parameter…” in either the Report Data pane or the Design pane, the Report Parameter Properties window will open. 

There are three main aspects which you must configure for every new parameter: General, Available Values, and Default Values. 
General
The General properties of a parameter are displayed when you open the Report Parameter Properties window. They include:
Property
Values
Notes
Name
Name of the parameter
This must exactly match the name of the parameter within the report SQL code; e.g. if your parameter is called PersonRef within the SQL code, it must be called PersonRef within the properties screen. 
Prompt
The user prompt
This can be whatever you like (although there are naming standards); e.g. the PersonRef parameter can have the prompt value of “Personnel number”. 
Data type
Text, Boolean, Date/Time, Integer, Float
The only values used within HR Reporting .RDL files are Text (for alphanumeric fields) and Date/Time for date parameters. 
Allow blank value (“”)
Ticked or unticked
This box should be ticked if the parameter is an optional free-text field which will pass a single value to the report query, e.g. Surname. This will allow report users to either specify a surname or to leave the Surname parameter blank before running a report.
Allow null value
Ticked or unticked
This box should be ticked if the parameter is an optional free-text field which will pass multiple values to the report query, e.g. Pay Code. This will allow report users to either specify a list of pay codes (‘135’,’247’,’630’) or to leave the Pay Code parameter blank before running a report. 
Allow multiple values
Ticked or unticked
This box should be ticked if the parameter is an optional list of values from which a user can select one, several, or none, e.g. Department Code. This will allow users to specify which department codes they wish to run the report for. T
Visibility
Visible, Hidden, Internal
All parameters are Visible by default, except the Username parameter, which is Hidden. 

Naming standards for prompts
In order to maintain a consistent look and feel across the HR Reporting catalogue, parameter prompts must follow certain naming standards. These are outlined below. 
The prompt for a person reference must always be Personnel number.
The word “description” is always omitted from prompt text; e.g. if the parameter is for “department description”, the prompt must be simply Department. 
Prompts of more than one word should only capitalise the first word; e.g. a prompt for the “employee status” value should be Employee status, not “Employee Status”. 

Available Values
If your parameter is powered by a drop-down list of values (LOV), you will need to define the LOV you want the parameter to use. Go to the Available Values tab of the Report Parameter Properties window:

Here you can either select a shared dataset from which to derive the LOV, or define the values yourself. 
If you’re using a shared dataset, select the option to “Get values from a query”, then complete the following fields: 
Property
Values
Notes
Dataset
Name of the shared dataset
Select this from the drop-down list. 
Value field
VALUE_FIELD
This must always be “VALUE_FIELD”.
Label field
LABEL_FIELD
This must always be “LABEL_FIELD”. 

If you’re not using a shared dataset, you can create your own list of values by selecting “Specify values” and completing the following fields:
Property
Values
Example
Label
The value you want to be displayed in the drop-down list.
“Oncology”
Value
The value you want the parameter to pass to the report SQL code when the query is run.
“AA”

It’s okay if the “Label” and “Value” fields match each other, but it’s better for a report’s performance to pass shorter strings to the SQL query as parameter values. 

In the example above, the department code (the value) “AA” is only two characters, while the department name (the label) “Oncology” is eight characters. Rather than passing “Oncology” as the parameter value, the report passes “AA” – which makes it run faster. 

If you want to give users the option to select “All [parameter values]”, you will need to specify that in your LOV as follows:
Label = < All [parameter values] > 
Value = -1 
This is important: if you don’t specify a “-1” value in your LOV, users will not be able to run the report for all possible parameter values without selecting every value in the LOV individually! 
Default Values
You can configure the default value(s) for your parameter by going to the Default Values tab of the Report Parameter Properties window:

Here you can either select a dataset from which to derive the default value(s), or define the value(s) yourself. 

Only the Username parameter uses a dataset to derive its default value. All other parameters either specify their own default values, or do not have default values. 
If you’re setting the default value for the Username parameter, select the option to “Get values from a query”, then complete the following fields: 
Property
Values
Notes
Dataset
CoreUser
Select this from the drop-down list. 
Value field
CoreUser
This is the only field in the “CoreUser” dataset; it returns the report user’s SSO username. 

If you’re setting the default value for any other parameter, select “Specify values” and complete the following fields:
Property
Values
Notes
Value
This will nearly always be -1
“-1” is the default value for nearly all drop-down LOV parameters. It tells the report query not to limit the results, but instead to return every possible value for the parameter, e.g. every possible department code. 

If you want to pass some other default value to the parameter, simply specify it in the Value field. You can add as many default values as you like: the purpose of a default value is to “pre-filter” a report for users so that they don’t have to select the most commonly-used values for parameters. A good example of this is the “Employee status” parameter, which uses several default values:

Free-text parameters, such as Personnel number and Surname, do not have default values; in those cases, you should simply select “No default value”. 
Once you have set all your parameter’s properties, click OK to close the Report Parameter Properties window. Enter CTRL+S to save your changes to the .RDL file.

Within the Parameters textbox
After adding your new parameter to the SQL code and the Parameters folder, you have the option to add it to the Parameters textbox. This is not required unless you want the new parameter to appear at the top of the report after the report is run, as shown in this example:

If you want your new parameter to appear at the top of the report, you’ll need to edit the VBA expression within the textbox. The textbox sits between the .RDL title text and the report Tablix: 

To edit it, right-click the box and select “Expression”: 

The Expression window will pop up. Within this window, you can create the VBA code which determines how each parameter is displayed within the textbox when the report is run. 

NB: It’s good practice to copy and paste the existing VBA code from another report with similar parameters; e.g. if you want to add a “Department Code” parameter, open the .RDL file for a report which already has a “Department Code” parameter and copy the VBA expression from that .RDL. You can modify the code as necessary for your own parameter(s) – this just saves you the trouble of writing the VBA from scratch.

The VBA expression
The VBA expression should always begin with the following code:
=Iif(Globals!RenderFormat.IsInteractive, "", Globals!ReportName + " - " ) +
"Selected parameters -- "

Once that code is in place, begin adding your parameters to the expression, following the guidance below. 

NB: The parameters in the textbox expression should be listed in the same order as they appear in the parameters table at the top of the Design pane (reading from left to right). If your parameters table looks like this:

…then your VBA expression should list the parameters as follows:
Payroll period
Pay codes
Personnel number

The Username parameter is hidden and is never included in the VBA expression. 
LOV parameters
Parameters which use a drop-down list of values should be added to the VBA expression with an “IIF” statement. IIF statements in VBA are IF-THEN-ELSE statements:
+IIF(this condition is true), display this string, otherwise display this string
Example: EmployeeStatus parameter

+ iif(Parameters!EmployeeStatus.Value(0) = "-1", 
", Employee status : '< All employee statuses >'",
", Employee status : '" + Join(Parameters!EmployeeStatus.Label, ", ") + "' ")
Remember that back in the Report Parameter Properties window, you set the parameter value field to “VALUE_FIELD” and the label field to “LABEL_FIELD”. You can refer to these two fields within your VBA expression, so that the expression looks at the VALUE_FIELD to determine what LABEL should be displayed in the textbox; e.g. if the VALUE for EmployeeStatus is “4”, the LABEL displayed in the textbox will be “WORKER”. 
Here’s that example again: 
+ iif(Parameters!EmployeeStatus.Value(0) = "-1", 
", Employee status : '< All employee statuses >'",
", Employee status : '" + Join(Parameters!EmployeeStatus.Label, ", ") + "' ")
You can modify this VBA to point to your own parameter by editing the parameter name within the formula to the name of the parameter you want to display. A list of available parameters is shown within the Expression window:

Free-text parameters (single- and multi-value)
Parameters which use a free-text field that accepts a single value, such as Personnel Number or Surname, should also be added to the VBA expression with an “IIF” statement, as shown above. 
The only difference between the VBA for free-text parameters and the VBA for drop-down LOV parameters is as follows:
For an LOV parameter, the IIF statement says if the parameter’s value is X, display the label Y:
+ iif(Parameters!EmployeeStatus.Value(0) = "-1", 
", Employee status : '< All employee statuses >'",
", Employee status : '" + Join(Parameters!EmployeeStatus.Label, ", ") + "' ")
For a free-text single-value parameter, the IIF statement says if the parameter’s value is X, display the value X:
+iif(Parameters!Surname.Value="",", 
Surname : '< All surnames >'",
", Surname : '" + Parameters!Surname.Value + "' ")

Likewise, for a free-text multi-value parameter, the IIF statement says if the parameter’s value is X, display the value X: 
+ iif(Parameters!DepartmentCode.Value="",
"Department code : '< All department codes >'",
"Department code : '" + Parameters!DepartmentCode.Value + "' ")

Date parameters
Parameters which only accept Date/Time values, such as Start Date or End Date, do not require an IIF statement; they should just display whatever value was entered by the user. You can add a date parameter to the VBA expression with this format:

+Prompt text + FORMAT(DateParameter.Value, “dd/MM/yyyy”) 

This code just sticks the parameter prompt text in front of whatever date the user selected for the parameter, and formats the date in dd/MM/yyyy style.

+"Period start date: '"+ FORMAT(Parameters!Period_start_date.Value,"dd/MM/yyyy") + "'"

Here’s an example from a completed report:

Once you’ve added your new parameter(s) to the Parameters textbox, be sure to enter CTRL+S to save your changes to the .RDL file. 

Editing an existing parameter
If you need to edit a parameter which already exists in an .RDL file, you’ll need to perform the following steps in the order displayed below: 
Edit the parameter within the SQL code and test the amended code within SQL Developer to ensure your amended parameter is working as expected.
If you’re happy with the updated SQL code, update the report query in the .RDL file with the new code.
Once you’ve changed the report query in the .RDL, you should amend the Report Parameter Properties for the parameter you have changed. Be sure to check the General, Available Values, and Default Values tabs to record your changes in all the relevant fields. 
After updating the Report Parameter Properties, check the Parameters textbox to see if the VBA expression needs amending to reflect your changes. 
Enter CTRL+S to save your changes to the .RDL when you are finished.

Removing a parameter
If a parameter is no longer required, you can remove it from the .RDL file.
Within the SQL code
First, you’ll need to amend the SQL for the report query to remove all references to the parameter. Remember that parameters are located in WHERE clauses (and WITH clauses in the case of free-text multi-value parameters), so check these parts of the SQL code first. 
Parameter values may be used in calculations or conditions elsewhere in the SQL, so don’t just look at the WHERE/WITH clauses! For complex reports, removing a parameter may require you to amend the SQL in multiple places. 
Once you’ve updated the SQL and tested that it works correctly, save your changes to the .RDL file. 
Within the Parameters folder
Now that the parameter is gone from the SQL, you need to remove it from the .RDL file. In the Report Data pane, go to the Parameters folder and select the parameter you want to remove. Right-click it and select “Delete”:

You can also remove parameters from the section at the top of the Design pane. Right-click the parameter you want to remove and select “Delete”: 

A warning message will pop up; click OK to confirm deletion:

Enter CTRL+S to save your changes to the .RDL file.
Within the Parameters textbox
If the parameter you are removing is referenced in the Parameters textbox, you’ll need to delete any lines of VBA code which refer to it. Right-click the textbox and select “Expression”: 

The Expression window will open. Select the line of VBA code you want to delete and hit “Delete” on your keyboard. 

Click OK to exit the Expression window and enter CTRL+S to save your changes to the .RDL file. 
Appendix: Free-text multi-value parameters
Many reports have free-text parameters which will accept multiple values in a comma-separated list, e.g. a list of pay codes. This enables report users to type in a list of the exact codes they want to see in the report, without having to scroll through a long drop-down LOV to select each code. 

The SQL which supports a free-text multi-value parameter is a little complicated, so here’s a worked example for the pay code parameter shown above. 
The WITH clause
Free-text multi-value parameters rely on something called a “WITH” clause, which is a bit of SQL which defines a temporary dataset whose output is available to be referenced in subsequent queries.
At the top of the appropriate SELECT statement in your report, add a WITH clause which includes your parameter. The format should be as follows:
(WITH temporary_dataset AS (SELECT :Parameter AS temporary_item FROM DUAL)

SELECT
…rest of SELECT statement… ) 
Example: 
(WITH paycodetext AS (SELECT :PayCode AS paycode_text FROM DUAL)

SELECT 
PABI_PAY_HISTORY.PAYROLL_PERIOD as PAYROLL_PERIOD… )
The WITH clause here has created a temporary view called paycodetext which contains a temporary item called paycode_text. The values available for the paycodetext.paycode_text item are defined by whatever the report user enters in the :PayCode parameter free-text field. 
The WHERE clause
Now that you’ve added your WITH clause, you can add the parameter to the appropriate WHERE clause in your report. 

NB: You’ll have to use the WHERE clause which belongs to the SELECT statement to which you added the WITH clause. Complex reports contain multiple SELECT statements and multiple WHERE clauses, so be sure to modify the appropriate WHERE clause!

In the WHERE clause, you’re going to refer back to the WITH clause you just created, using the following format:
WHERE
(VIEW.ITEM IN 
(SELECT 
UPPER(regexp_substr(temporary_dataset.temporary_item, '[^, ]+', 1,LEVEL))
FROM temporary_dataset
CONNECT BY INSTR(temporary_dataset.temporary_item,',', 1, LEVEL - 1) > 0) 
OR (:Parameter) IS NULL) 

Example: 

WHERE
(PABI_PAY_HISTORY.PAY_CODE IN 
(SELECT 
UPPER(regexp_substr(paycodetext.paycode_text, '[^, ]+', 1,LEVEL)) 
FROM paycodetext
CONNECT BY instr(paycodetext.paycode_text, ',', 1, LEVEL - 1) > 0) 
OR (:PayCode) IS NULL)

This bit of code tells the report to return records where the PABI_PAY_HISTORY.PAY_CODE is included in the temporary paycodetext dataset. It also tells the report how to “read” the paycodetext dataset, which is just a comma-separated list. The regexp_substr() and instr() functions are essentially telling the report to create a new row in paycodetext every time it encounters a comma, so that this list:

…gets transformed into this table:

paycodetext
233
256
348

The report should return any records where the PABI_PAY_HISTORY.PAY_CODE is included in this temporary table. 

The NULL option
If the user doesn’t want to specify any pay codes, they need to tick the “NULL” box next to the parameter. 

This tells the report to ignore the parameter and skip all the code described above. 

NB: For free-text multi-value parameters, users must either enter some values or select “NULL”; they cannot leave the field blank. If they do leave the field blank, the report will try create a temporary dataset that contains zero rows, and to use that as the basis for the parameter – which won’t work.

This document provides information that you will need when working in Oracle SQL Developer, including how to launch the application, how to navigate around it, and an explanation of commonly-used terms. This is not a process document so much as a “contextual information” document which you may find useful when you initially begin creating and editing reports in SQL Developer. 

Getting Started with SQL Developer 
Before you can create or edit reports, you will need to launch the Oracle SQL Developer application and connect to the PeopleXD database you wish to query. 

SQL Developer is a remote desktop application. You can find it in your Start menu under “CONNECT Remote Services (RADC)”:

Double-click the entry in your Start menu to launch SQL Developer, and enter your CONNECT login details when prompted – these are necessary in order to access the CONNECT Remote Desktop:

After a short wait, the SQL Developer splash screen will appear, and the application will load:

You’ll land on the Welcome Page, which contains links to any databases to which you have previously connected, as well as links to Oracle resources for SQL Developer users. The only thing you’ll generally use here is the Database Connection pane:

If you have existing database connections, you can simply click on the database to which you wish to connect, and SQL Developer will open a worksheet for you in a new tab, where you can begin querying the database. 
If you’ve never used SQL Developer before, you will need to create the database connections you require. This is done by setting up something called a connection profile. See below for details. 
Creating connection profiles
To create a connection profile, click the link on the Welcome Page to “Create a Connection Manually”:

A pop-up window will open. Populate it as described below.

Field
Value
Notes
Name
The name you want to assign to the database connection.

You can test your new connection profile by clicking the “Test” button at the bottom of the pop-up window:

A little progress window will open while SQL Developer tries to contact the database:

Using SQL Worksheets
In order to run reports in SQL Developer, you need to use a worksheet. A worksheet is a page where you write (or copy-paste) the SQL code that you’ll use to query the PeopleXD database. When you launch SQL Developer and connect to a database, SQL Developer opens a worksheet for you automatically in a new tab:

If you’re building a new report (or simply running a small query of some kind), you can simply type your SQL code into the worksheet. If you’ve got the SQL code for an existing report, you can paste it into the worksheet. 

Once you’ve got your code in place, click the little green arrow at the top of the worksheet to execute the code: 

SQL Developer will read the code you’ve entered in the worksheet and will query the PeopleXD database for the information you’ve requested. This may take some time, depending on how complicated the query is, so you might see this progress bar whilst SQL Developer works:

Once SQL Developer has finished executing the code, the results of the query will be displayed in the Query Result pane at the bottom of the screen. 

Exporting the results
You may wish to export the results of your SQL query to an Excel file for further analysis. To do this, right-click anywhere in the Query Results pane and select “Export…” from the pop-up menu:

The Export Wizard will open. You need to specify what file format you wish to export the results to, and where on the network you want the export to be saved. In the “Format” field, select “csv”, and in the “File” field, enter the file-path for the network location to which you are exporting the results:

Note: Never export results to the Desktop or C:\ drive. 

SQL Developer is a remote desktop application – you would be exporting results to the remote desktop, not to your own PC! This is a security risk. It also makes it very difficult to access the file once it’s finished exporting!
Click “Next >” and then “Finish” to exit the Export Wizard. 

SQL Developer will begin exporting the results to a .csv file. You can view the progress of the export process in the Task Progress pane at the bottom of the screen:

If you can’t see the Task Progress pane, you might need to switch it on. You can find it in the View menu:

It’s a useful tool, especially if you’re exporting a very large result-set comprised of thousands of rows, as it allows you to check whether the export process is still running. It also provides a running count of how many rows of data have been exported, which may enable you to estimate when the export should be finished (e.g. if you know there are approximately 1,000 rows of data and the Task Progress pane shows that 500 rows have been exported in 30 seconds, you can safely assume that the remaining 500 rows will be exported in the next 30 seconds). 
The Task Progress pane will go blank once the export process is complete.

Navigate to the location to which you exported the result-set to check that the file has been saved there as expected:

You’ve now successfully run a SQL query and exported the results to Excel!

Entering the database

Tables are datasets organised by columns and rows. The columns are the “attributes” of the table – things like PERSON_REFERENCE and SURNAME. The rows are where the “records” are stored.

This document provides information that you will need when working in Visual Studio, including how to launch the application, how to navigate around it, and an explanation of commonly-used terms. This is not a process document so much as a “contextual information” document which you may find useful when you initially begin creating and editing reports in Visual Studio. 

Commonly-used terms
There are a number of commonly-used terms that appear throughout this document. A brief explanation of each is given here.

Term
Notes

A dataset is the SQL code which queries the PeopleXD database and returns results. It can be embedded (unique to a single .RDL file) or shared (available to re-use across multiple .RDL files). 
“DataSet1” within any .RDL file contains the report SQL code.

An embedded dataset is a SQL query which is unique to a single .RDL file.

Launching Visual Studio 
Before you can create or edit reports, you will need to launch the Visual Studio application and select the solution file (.sln) that you want to work in. 

Visual Studio is a remote desktop application. You can find it in your Start menu under “CONNECT Remote Services (RADC)”:

Double-click the entry in your Start menu to launch Visual Studio, and enter your CONNECT login details when prompted – these are necessary in order to access the CONNECT Remote Desktop:

A little RemoteApp pop-up window will run while the application launches – this may be present for as long as a few minutes, so be patient: 

After a short wait, the Visual Studio splash screen will appear, followed by a sign-in window. Click the “Not now, maybe later” link at the bottom of the sign-in window: 

You’ll then be asked for your display preferences. Select Development Settings: General and click Start Visual Studio to complete the app launch. 

After another short wait (occasionally as long as a minute or two), Visual Studio will open and you will see the Home screen:

Navigating Visual Studio
Once you’ve successfully launched Visual Studio, you will need to navigate to the solution file you want to work in before you can create or amend reports, data sets, or data sources. See below for guidance on how to find your way around Visual Studio. 
Solution files (.SLNs)
Files in Visual Studio are grouped into larger files called “solutions” (file extension .sln). A solution is effectively a “bucket” in which related files can be stored – there’s a lot more to this concept, but the important thing to remember is that each solution has its own data sources, datasets, and report files. 
There are four HR Reporting solutions for you to choose from in Visual Studio.

Moving files in Visual Studio 
You may at times need to move a file from one solution to another in Visual Studio (usually a report .RDL, but occasionally a shared dataset .RSD). Deploying files from Visual Studio
Whenever you create a new shared dataset or report in Visual Studio, you will need to deploy it to the HR Reporting environments to make it available to report users. The deployment process is the same across all HR Reporting solutions and environments, and the steps are outlined below. 

To deploy a file, select it in the Solution Explorer pane and right-click. Select “Deploy” from the right-click menu:

The progress of the deployment will display in the Output pane at the bottom of your screen. Look at the final message to see whether your deployment has succeeded or failed:
